title: Review: planning a night out
why: This review brings together all the present-tense irregulars from the unit (ir, venir, salir, hacer, querer, poder, tener que, saber, conocer, the stem changers) and sorts them into families. You'll put them to work suggesting, accepting or turning down plans in Seville, weather included, before heading into town in the next unit.

Recap: present-tense irregulars

In five lessons, you've seen all the common present-tense irregulars. To remember them, sort them into families: it's much easier than learning them one by one.

FamilyWhat changesVerbs
-goonly yotengo, vengo, salgo, hago, pongo, digo
-zcoonly yoconozco
yo in -oyonly yosoy, estoy, voy, doy
one of a kindonly yosé
e → iethe bootquiero, pienso, empiezo, prefiero, cierro
o → uethe bootpuedo, duermo, vuelvo, encuentro, cuesta
e → ithe bootpido, repito, sirvo, sigo
u → uethe bootjuego

Double trouble

Three verbs have both irregularities: a g in the first person and a vowel change in the other “boot” forms (ie for tener and venir, i for decir).

tenervenirdecir
yotengovengodigo
tútienesvienesdices
él, ella, ustedtienevienedice
nosotros, nosotrastenemosvenimosdecimos
vosotros, vosotrastenéisvenísdecís
ellos, ellas, ustedestienenvienendicen

And ir is in a class of its own: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. It's the most irregular verb, and also the most useful one for suggesting a night out.

", "

Suggesting, accepting, turning down

A handful of phrases is all you need to make plans. They use every verb from the unit.

To…You sayEnglish
suggest¿Quieres venir al cine?Do you want to come to the movies?
suggest¿Vamos a la playa el sábado?Shall we go to the beach on Saturday?
suggest¿Por qué no vamos al parque?Why don't we go to the park?
accept¡Vale! / ¡Genial! / Sí, claro.OK! / Great! / Yes, of course.
turn downLo siento, no puedo: tengo que trabajar.Sorry, I can't: I have to work.
suggest something elsePrefiero ir a la piscina.I'd rather go to the pool.
set the time¿A qué hora quedamos?What time shall we meet?
set the place¿Dónde quedamos? Quedamos en la plaza.Where shall we meet? Let's meet in the square.

Quedar

Quedar (a regular -ar verb) means “to meet up, to arrange to meet.” Spaniards use it all the time when making plans: Quedamos a las ocho en la puerta del cine. It's close to the English “meet up,” but it also covers the arranging part: one word for “let's meet” and “we're meeting.”

Lo siento (I'm sorry) is a set phrase: learn it as it is. Notice that Spanish uses the present tense for plans where English often says “shall we…?” or “let's…”: a plain present-tense question is all you need.

¿Vamos al concierto el viernes? Lo siento, el viernes no puedo.Shall we go to the concert on Friday? Sorry, I can't on Friday.
", "

The weather and plan B

Plans often depend on the weather. Remember: hace + noun, with mucho before the noun. Where English says “it's hot” with an adjective, Spanish literally says “it makes a lot of heat.”

SpanishEnglish
Hace sol y hace mucho calor.It's sunny and it's very hot.
Hace buen tiempo.The weather's nice.
Hace frío y hace viento.It's cold and windy.
Llueve.It's raining.

Si llueve…

For a plan B, Spanish uses si + present tense, exactly like English: Si llueve, vamos al cine (if it rains, we'll go to the movies). Si without an accent means “if”; sí with an accent means “yes.”

Seville in practice

  • In summer, afternoons are scorching: people in Seville go out late, often after ten at night.
  • A favorite place to meet is a square or the riverside, along el río Guadalquivir.
  • The Triana neighborhood, across the river, is famous for flamenco and tapas bars.
Si hace mucho calor, quedamos a las diez de la noche en Triana.If it's very hot, let's meet at ten at night in Triana.
